question: What are the najasat (ritual impurities), and what are their rulings?
asked: When we were doing the talk on the Barzakh, we mentioned the Prophet ﷺ saying that most of the punishment of the grave is from not being careful with najasat. Can you please remind us what the najasat are and what the rulings for them are?
answer:
So, basic fiqh, simple question. It's a standard question. In fact, all of the books of fiqh, the very first few chapters always talk about the najasat. And obviously my answer today will be summarizing, but for detailed studies, choose your madhhab and choose a fiqh book. So I'll briefly summarize.

Najasat: Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala tells us in the Qur'an, of the earliest of revelations:

> وَثِيَابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ

One of the first commandments in the Qur'an, which our scholars have interpreted to mean that we cannot have najas on our clothes and our body. And the shari'ah has come with assigning certain substances to be impure.

When we say impure, what is meant is that we are not allowed to pray to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala with the najas on our clothing or body. This does not mean that najas can never touch us. It is permissible to touch najas for a hajah, a darurah; it is permissible when we need to do that. A mother — or a father these days, mashallah, as well — changing diapers, they're going to touch najas. Okay, that's what happens. It's not haram per se to get in contact with najas, but it is makruh to do so for no reason, and **it is haram to pray while the najas is on your body knowingly**.

So the sin is incurred, and the punishment of the qabr, is only linked to the salah. It is not linked outside of salah. If a person has a need to touch najasat — that's their job, that's the occupation, they are responsible for something — then that is not a sin per se. And otherwise, other than this, it is makruh to have any najas on us overall.

So to summarize what are the najasat. There is nothing najas that grows from the earth. All plants, all vegetation, all natural products, rocks and stones: there is no najasah amongst them. As well, according to the dominant position, there is nothing najas from the ocean. Even a dead fish is not najas. Anything from the ocean is pure.

One of the main controversies from the time of the Sahabah is over the urine and the excrement of animals that are eaten, ma'kul al-lahm. The animals that are not eaten — lions, tigers, bears — their excrement, that is najas. But the animals that are eaten — camels, sheep, cows, goats — that is the classic controversy, and the majority position is that they are not najas. That's the majority position. They're herbivores, and so they're not najas. And the evidence for this: the Prophet ﷺ said, pray in the pens of sheep. Where sheep reside, you may pray in that. So from this it is known — sheep pens have their excrement and whatnot. In any case, that's a controversy. Some of the madhhabs get out of this and they say that it is najis.

As well, there is a controversy over the urine of a baby boy who is still being breastfed. Three of the madhhabs, other than the Hanafis, say the urine of a baby boy is not najis. The reason for this is an explicit hadith that the Prophet ﷺ said: you may sprinkle over the urine of a baby boy, and you must wash the urine of a baby girl. Why? We have no reason. It's just that the shari'ah has come with it. So if a baby boy is still feeding naturally, you know, its mother's milk — of course those days they didn't have diapers — but in case the urine has leaked out, the Prophet ﷺ said you can just sprinkle some water. You can still wear the clothes; it's not going to be najis. Whereas if it is from a girl, or it is an adult or a toddler that is eating and drinking, then it will be najas. Obviously adult and toddler human excrement and waste is, by unanimous consensus, najas.

With regards to dead animals: dead animals are all najas if they are blood animals. As for animals that are not blood, like insects or whatnot, these are disgusting but not najas. There's a difference between the two. You don't want it, but it's not najas per se. A dead insect, for example, is not najis. The najasah comes from animals that have blood, that are dead. So any animal that has blood and it is a maytah — not a sacrifice; it's a natural death or a death by another animal — every maytah is najis.

Living animals: again there is a controversy, but by unanimous consensus the pig is najis in totality. As for the dog — maybe one day I'll give a longer lecture on it, because we live in a society where we're surrounded by those canines — but as for the issue of the najasah of the dog, there is a whole spectrum of controversy. And again, in this brief talk I'm just going over it very, very quickly. Some madhhabs say nothing about the dog is najas, primarily the Maliki madhhab. Ibn Taymiyyah and some of the Hanafi scholars said that the skin and the fur of the dog is not najis; only the saliva is najis. And this is a very strong opinion; it is the opinion that I also give fatwa on. Ibn Taymiyyah strongly argued this: that if a dog brushes against you, the skin of the dog is not najis. What is najis is the saliva of the dog, if the dog licks, if the dog puts its tongue in it. And many of the other scholars said everything about the dog is najis, just like the pig. So there's that controversy over there.

Otherwise, most other animals, other than these two, their skin is not considered najas. The only controversy is over dogs, and as for pigs, it is najasah by unanimous consensus. Cats, by explicit hadith, are not najas, even their saliva. Our Prophet ﷺ — explicit hadith, it is in Bukhari and Muslim — allowed us to use the water that the cats had drunk from. We can use it to do wudu and whatnot; there is no problem with that.

From human bodies: obviously stool and urine, we mentioned. The other things that come out are madhi and wadi. Madhi is the fluid that is released in the state of sexual excitement, called pre-seminal fluid, and this is najis according to all of the scholars of Islam. Wadi is a whitish fluid that comes out because of a medical issue, and again this is considered to be najis as well. It is not typical, it is not common, but it is a medical issue that sometimes happens.

The controversy comes over the male ejaculation, or the seminal fluid. Two of the madhhabs say it is not najas, believe it or not; two of the madhhabs say it is najas. The Shafi'is and the Hanbalis say that the male fluid is not najasah, and they say: how can it be najas when man is created from it? And Allah says in the Qur'an:

> وَلَقَدْ كَرَّمْنَا بَنِي آدَمَ

How can Allah create us from that which is najas? And the other two madhhabs say that it is najas. So again, there is that controversy over that issue, and Allah knows best. But the position I follow, humbly, as well: generally, it is not najas.

What is najasah as well from the body is flowing blood. Now this is very important; a lot of people get confused. Spots of blood, a nosebleed, just that comes out: all the scholars say a small amount, yasir ad-dam, is forgiven. A prick, a paper cut, some nosebleed: this is forgiven. What is not forgiven in terms of najasah is daman masfuhan, because the Qur'an mentions gushing blood, flowing blood. That blood you cannot pray in unless it is darurah. Like 'Umar radiyAllahu 'anhu: they mention when he was stabbed to death, he prayed in that state. This is a darurah; what are you going to do? I mean, if you're a prisoner or something, that's a darurah. Otherwise, flowing blood is considered to be najas, and this is pretty much the majority position.

With regards to leather — again, maybe one day I'll give a longer lecture — there are, believe it or not, nine opinions about leather. Nine different opinions about leather; a very big issue of debate amongst the classical fuqaha. We are most concerned about pig leather, because we don't use dog leather or anything like this. There is a minor controversy. Abu Hanifah's most famous student, Abu Yusuf, and a number of scholars claimed that there is no najasah in leather. So Abu Yusuf, the student of Abu Hanifah, would give the fatwa — and this is not just his; a number of prominent scholars said — that once you tan leather (actually not dried; tanned leather is the precise term), once you tan leather, they say, it ceases being najis, even if the origin is najis.

The dominant position is that pig will always be najis, whether it is alive, whether it is dead. And no doubt it is best to avoid pig leather, and Allah knows best. No doubt it is best to avoid it, just to get out. And this would also include the bristles of the pig, which are used in very fancy combs. You know, some really fancy combs have boar hair, boar bristles. So this would also be there. If you follow Abu Yusuf's position, it is permissible, but the dominant position of our shari'ah, of the madhahib, is that it would not be considered permissible.

The other controversy was over alcohol. By alcohol we mean, obviously, khamr, which is ethanol, everything that intoxicates. And again, this is an issue of controversy. The dominant position, definitely in early and medieval Islam, is that khamr is najis. However, believe it or not, it's one of those opinions that modern fiqh councils have pretty much reversed, by and large, and there are many reasons for this beyond the scope of our talk today. The dominant fatwa in our times, by almost all major fiqh councils, is that ethanol is not najas.

And the fact of the matter is, there are explicit evidences in the seerah, in the hadith. The most famous one: when alcohol was made haram, what did the Sahabah do? They threw it in the streets. And the riwayat say: we could smell, we were walking, the streets flowed with khamr for two, three days. You are not allowed to dispose of najasah in the streets. You cannot just throw something outside where people are walking. And the Sahabah did this, which demonstrates they understood khamr is haram to drink, but it is not najis.

Poison is haram; it's not najis. Not everything haram is najis, you understand, obviously. Gambling is haram, but it's not najis; the gambling tokens are not najis per se. So the point being that by saying ethanol is not najis, this means all of these soap dispenser things, the hand sanitizers, and in the hospital — what do you call it — the wipes, when they put the medicine and all that. Because if you say that alcohol or ethanol is najis, then you are basically saying all of those hand sanitizers and the cleansing of the hospitals would be a type of najis. You cannot use any needle, anything. It's a really big haraj, right? And when you look at it technically, there are many evidences to show that ethanol is not najas. Also, the perfumes that we apply have ethanol in them. It is not najas. It is permissible to apply, because you are not consuming that ethanol.

So this is a quick, brief history, or a summary, of najasat. In all of these, the strictest najas, there are three that are above and beyond the other things:

1. Everything to do with a pig. That is the worst type of najasah.
2. The saliva of a dog is the second worst type of najasah.
3. The menstrual blood. That is the third type, which is the worst of the najasat.

Then you have all of the najasat in one category. Then you have the urine of a baby boy, the slightest type, because it's not quite najas, but it is still not quite pure; you have to still sprinkle water on it.

So this is a brief summary of the najasat. As we said, what is haram and sinful is to pray when any of these substances is knowingly on you. If it is unknowing, obviously you are forgiven:

> لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا

But if it is known, and you don't care to take precautions, and you stand up to pray, this is where 'adhab al-qabr comes. Especially for urine, because out of all of this list, it is urine that every single human being is interacting with on a daily basis. So if you do not take care and you're careless — splattering, not cleansing oneself — that is where the 'adhab al-qabr punishment comes into place, because it shows you don't care about the shari'ah of Allah.

Before we move on to the second question, an important disclaimer. A lot of people do not know that the shari'ah does not require water when we do istinja. This is a shock to most Muslims to learn. In reality there is zero controversy, by unanimous consensus of all of the madhahib and scholars of Islam: even if you have gallons of water next to you, you are not required to use water in the restroom, either for urine or even for defecation. It is not a requirement. It is better. It is mustahabb, and we thank Allah. In our cultures people think it is wajib. It's good, but technically it is not wajib. Technically it is not required. You may use anything that is dry, that dries that area, until no traces are left.

Why do I say this? I'm not saying you stop using the lota. Keep the lota, install the lota, get the hand lota — it's only $20 — install it, very good. If you're in Europe, even better, they have the bidet system, which is even better. I'm not saying don't use it. Why am I telling you this? Because a lot of people, when they are not at home or within Muslim houses, they're stopping in the restrooms in public places, they assume that khalas, this is najis, simply using the restroom without having your handy lota with you, right? They think that, khalas, I cannot pray. And this is a very serious fiqh error.

**You do not need water to be pure after going to the restroom.** Toilet paper does the job. You keep on wiping until no traces are left, until it is dry and no traces are left, and that applies even to defecation as well. There's no problem. In fact, the default amongst the Sahabah: they would not choose water. Even when they had water, they wouldn't use it, because it was just a hassle; they would have to carry it. They wouldn't use it; they would use just the materials out there. These days the toilet paper suffices. So just because you stop in the restroom on the way between places and whatnot, don't think that you're in a state of najasah.

And by the way, you can use toilet paper, put it under the sink, and mashallah, you have a portable lota. So you can even do that if need be. But my point is, even if you don't use water, it is still pure and tahir, meaning you're not in a state of najasah, and you may pray in that state.
